subject: math
domain: Conditional Probability and the Rules of Probability
cluster: Use the rules of probability to compute probabilities of compound events in a uniform probability model

items.prompt: To compute $P(A\mid B)$ from counts, divide count of $A$-and-$B$ by count of:
Of $20$ music students, $8$ play a sport. $P(\text{sport}\mid\text{music})$:
Of $12$ dog owners, $3$ have a cat. $P(\text{cat}\mid\text{dog})$:
A die is greater than $3$. Probability it is even:
A die is odd. Probability it is a $1$:
A die is even. Probability it is greater than $3$:
Of $40$ adults, $10$ bike and of those $4$ also hike. $P(\text{hike}\mid\text{bike})$:
A die is rolled; given it is at most $2$, probability it is a $1$:
Of $30$ students, $18$ passed; of those, $9$ got an A. $P(\text{A}\mid\text{pass})$:
A card is a heart ($13$ hearts); the probability it is the ace of hearts given it is a heart:
Of $50$ people, $20$ exercise; of those $5$ smoke. $P(\text{smoke}\mid\text{exercise})$:
A die is greater than $2$. Probability it is a $5$:
Explain why computing $P(A\mid B)$ divides by the count of $B$, not the grand total.
items.answer: Conditioning on $B$ means we already know $B$ happened, so the set of relevant outcomes shrinks to just those in $B$; the fraction of those that also satisfy $A$ uses the count of $B$ as the denominator.

steps: The known event $B$ becomes the new whole.
